analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on investment profits for individuals, retroactive to that summer.
analysis.headline: The capital gains tax cut never got a vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top tax rate on capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, or property held more than a year — from 20% to 15%, and cut the rate for taxpayers in lower income brackets from 10% to 7.5%, retroactive to June 24, 1998 [S2][S3]. It would also apply those lower rates under the alternative minimum tax and shorten the holding period needed for the lower rate from 18 months to 1 year [S3]. Speaker Newt Gingrich introduced it with 121 Republican cosponsors, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it and it died when the Congress ended [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households that sell appreciated assets at a profit — above all higher-income investors, who realize the large majority of taxable capital gains and pay the top rate the bill cuts from 20% to 15% [S3]. The bill also benefits business owners selling companies, real estate holders, and the securities and mutual fund industry, which would see more selling and trading as investors respond to lower rates [S3]. The retroactive effective date means gains booked after June 24, 1998 get the cut immediately [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum individual capital gains rate from 20% to 15%, so a taxpayer selling appreciated assets pays no more than 15% on most long-term gains [S3].
Cuts the capital gains rate for taxpayers in lower income-tax brackets from 10% to 7.5%, a modest benefit to small investors and mutual fund shareholders [S3].
Applies the same reduced 7.5%/15% rates under the alternative minimum tax, so the cut is not clawed back for investors subject to the AMT [S3].
Makes the cut retroactive to June 24, 1998, with special transition rules so gains and losses taken into account after that date are taxed under the new, lower rates [S3].
Shortens the holding period required for the lower long-term rate from 18 months to 1 year, letting investors qualify for the reduced rate sooner [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which would collect less revenue on every qualifying asset sale, with the largest share of the cut going to the higher-income filers who pay the top rate. All taxpayers ultimately bear that cost through higher future taxes, a larger deficit, or reduced public spending; the bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions [S3].

drawbacks.text: A capital gains rate cut reduces federal revenue with no offset in the bill, adding to the deficit or forcing cuts or tax increases elsewhere [S3].

The benefit is concentrated at the top: higher-income households realize most taxable capital gains and pay the 20% top rate being cut to 15%, so most of the money goes to them rather than to the lower-bracket investors whose rate falls only from 10% to 7.5% [S3].
Retroactivity to June 24, 1998 hands an immediate windfall to investors for gains already realized, rather than encouraging new investment [S3].
Shortening the required holding period from 18 months to 1 year makes it easier to flip assets quickly for the reduced rate, tilting the tax code further toward investment income over wages [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers its largest benefits to the households that need them least: the top-rate cut from 20% to 15% dwarfs the small 10%-to-7.5% relief for lower-bracket investors, and the retroactive date converts what is nominally an investment incentive into an immediate windfall for sales already made. The cost — reduced federal revenue with no offset — is borne by everyone. As tax policy, it is a targeted transfer to asset owners dressed as growth policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended without the House ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Speaker Newt Gingrich introduced the bill on June 24, 1998, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 121 cosponsors, all of them Republicans — a majority of the House Republican caucus — but no Democrats [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or reported the bill; after the June 24, 1998 referral, the action history shows no further action of any kind [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee without a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and taxpayers generally, who kept the revenue that would have gone mainly to higher-income investors selling appreciated assets. High-income asset holders and the securities industry lost the tax cut they were seeking.

for.name: Newt Gingrich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill himself, with the 20%-to-15% capital gains cut as its sole provision

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred to his committee; no markup was ever held and the bill was never reported

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed further capital gains tax cuts in 1998 and vetoed a separate Republican tax bill that contained capital gains provisions

sides.party_line_note: All 121 cosponsors were Republicans and none were Democrats, though the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would have tested the split.

industries.note: The bill cuts the top capital gains rate from 20% to 15% retroactively, delivering its largest benefit to the households that sell the most appreciated assets. The revenue they no longer pay is a cost shared by every other taxpayer.

industries.industry: Securities, brokerage, and mutual fund industry
industries.note: Lower rates and a shorter holding period would encourage more selling and trading, raising fee and fund business. Ordinary small investors in mutual funds would also pay less tax, but the industry's broader gain rides on a tax cut whose revenue cost falls on everyone else.

Property held just one year would qualify for the reduced 15% rate instead of facing the 18-month requirement, making it cheaper to flip or sell appreciated real estate. Mainstream homeowners who already qualify for the existing exclusion see little change.
